prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: read-annotations
Deck beneath it: A reader's pencilled notes, left on the scanned pages, are gathered up and sorted into the three lists the mill acts on.

Hero: an old book lies open across the upper middle of the page, and rising from its pages a small flock of paper slips — the reader's notes — drift up and rightward like leaves in a breeze. Each slip carries one short handwritten word or phrase: one reads rotate, pinned to a small sketch of a sideways picture on the page below it; one reads no sky, pinned to a landscape picture whose top edge is marked with a gentle protective arc; several carry chapter names in a reader's hand. A note near the flock: the notes were left by hand, one per page, while paging through the scan.

The slips descend on the right into a sorting rack of three labeled pigeonholes, drawn as a small wooden letter-rack: the first hole labeled rotate holds slips beside a curved turning arrow; the second labeled no sky holds slips beside the little protected horizon; the third and deepest, labeled chapters, holds a neat stack of title slips with their page numbers showing as small tabs — 9, 23, 47. A note at the rack: a note that is not a turn mark or a sky mark is taken to be a chapter's title.

Below the rack, the outcome: a single ruled report sheet with three short grouped lists written down its length, captioned — the sorted lists, ready to be copied into the project's manifest, where the image cutter and the chapter splitter obey them.

One quiet observation at the lower left: a pencil resting on the open book beside one freshly written slip, captioned — the only handwork in the mill: a human reads the book and leaves the marks.

One warm accent colour follows the slips from page to pigeonhole to list; the book, rack, and report stay in ink.
